title_en: Why Laser Beams Are the Hottest New Tech in Defense
title_zh: 激光束为何成为国防领域最炙手可热的新技术——对话 Bloomberg Intelligence 的 Wayne Sanders
subtitle_zh: 从激光到微波武器，Bloomberg Intelligence 资深国防分析师拆解定向能武器如何重塑防空的经济账。
summary_zh: 本期 Odd Lots 中，Tracy Alloway 与 Joe Weisenthal 对话 Bloomberg Intelligence 资深国防研究分析师 Wayne Sanders，拆解国防领域最炙手可热的定向能武器（directed energy weapons）——高能激光与高功率微波（high powered microwaves）。核心是一笔经济账：用造价数百万美元的精密拦截弹去击落廉价、甚至用泡沫塑料和胶合板拼成的无人机并不划算，而激光与微波像深弹药（deep munition）、如同武器世界的可再生能源，一旦建成便可持续发射。但嘉宾强调这并非万能药：面对拥有高超音速武器（hypersonic weapons）的对手，仍须保留 Lockheed PAC-3、RTX SM-3/SM-6 等精密导弹，形成一体化防空与导弹防御。节目梳理了从千瓦到兆瓦的功率阶梯、中红外先进化学激光（MIRACL）等历史项目、稀土与镓等供应链约束，以及主承包商与 Anduril 等技术颠覆者在中端市场的分工和遍地的合资企业（joint ventures）。结论是稀缺性只是从弹药转移到别处，激光束并非终结防空难题的银弹。

If it's going slow enough or you have enough of them, you may want to then partner that with a high-powered microwave. to knock them down. So you don't want to give up any ground at all in terms of creation of these different capabilities. So these end up being additive. And Israel does it better than anyone. When you look at Israel, if you have an intercontinental ballistic missile threat that's coming your way, they're going to use their Arrow 2, Arrow 3 systems, which are exo-atmospheric. They're going to try and shoot this thing down as far away from you as possible and based off of how serious the threat is. If it's something else that's a little bit shorter than that, they have a system called David's Sling. And David's Sling goes farther than Iron Dome. Iron Dome is that next layer that you use, and you hear about it all the time between Iran and Israel in the 12-Day War, as well as during Epic Fury and into the systems now, is they continue to use Iron Dome. And now they're adding in Iron Beam as well. So what it's done is it gives the commander options, so that you don't always have to use your exquisite munitions. You don't have to bankrupt yourself to do it.
turns.zh: 而且，顺便说一句，当你面对以 Mach 5、也就是每小时 4,000 英里飞行的对手方能力时，你恐怕不会指望自己能把这束激光精确地放到你想要的位置上去做到这一点。所以你真正要找的是分层防空（layered air defense），对吧？我前面把它称为一体化防空与导弹防御。这一点之所以非常重要，是因为它跟我们此刻谈论的东西高度相关，尤其当你也看投资层面时。你必须保留精密导弹（exquisite missiles），你必须保留你的 Lockheed PAC-3 拦截弹，你必须保留你的 RTX SM-3 和 SM-6，你不能把它们淘汰掉，因为你有拥有高超音速武器（hypersonic weapons）的对手。如果一枚高超音速武器被发射，你会想用你更精密的能力之一去确保把它从空中击落，别让它杀死你的士兵、飞行员、水兵、海军陆战队员和你的太空军（guardians）。你要确保那种事不发生。所以精密导弹是这场对话的一部分。但最大的那块，就像你现在说的，是你意识到：你可以赢下每一次交战，在防御上赢下每一次交战，却在经济上输掉。这正是我们现在在 Iran 大量看到的——他们就是在开始耗尽我们的这些精密拦截弹和弹药。所以，正如你提到的 Coyote、你提到的 Vampire，BAE 有一个叫 APKWS 的系统，即先进精确杀伤武器系统（Advanced Precision Kill Weapon System）；Rheinmetall 有 Skynex 和 Skyranger。这些是更便宜的拦截弹和 gun。所以把它们想成是几乎一种中程解决方案，用来表明：好，我不想用一发 400 万美元的——因为你能看到雷达系统本身，如果有什么东西被发射并朝你飞来，它会拼出一个特征信号（signature），会说，这是这种类型的系统，正以这种速度朝我们射来，它会有助推段（boost phase）、滑翔段（glide phase）、末段（terminal phase），取决于这些能力是什么样的，对吧？重要的是能够说，好，那么，基于这个威胁，我想给它配一种说得通的、特定类型的能力。所以如果你正被射击，如果一群无人机蜂群朝你飞来、是出自 Iran 的 Shahed-136，你不需要用 PAC-3 拦截弹去击落它。你可能要找的是那个 Vampire、APKWS 的组合，你可能想用一些 Coyote Block II。你要去看这些系统，然后说，这就是我想用的。如果它飞得足够慢，或者你面对的数量足够多，你可能还想再配上高功率微波去把它们打下来。所以在创造这些不同能力方面，你一点都不想放弃阵地。所以这些最终是叠加式（additive）的。而 Israel 做得比谁都好。看 Israel，如果你有一枚洲际弹道导弹（intercontinental ballistic missile）威胁朝你飞来，他们会用他们的 Arrow 2、Arrow 3 系统，那是大气层外（exo-atmospheric）的，他们会尽可能在离你远的地方把这东西打下来，并根据威胁有多严重来决定。如果是比那稍微短程一点的东西，他们有个叫 David's Sling 的系统，而 David's Sling 比 Iron Dome 打得更远。Iron Dome 是你用的再下一层，你在 Iran 与 Israel 之间的 12-Day War、以及 Epic Fury 期间和如今的系统里一直听到它——他们持续使用 Iron Dome，现在又加入了 Iron Beam。所以它做的，是给了指挥官更多选项，这样你就不必总是动用你的精密弹药，不必为了做到这一点而把自己搞破产。

turns.en: If you have this integrated architecture that goes across all these different weapon systems for the reasons you just laid out, who actually makes or owns, I guess, the kill decision? Like who decides what deployment of all those different things actually looks like against which targets? And I imagine most of the time you're operating under like highly pressurized time environments, right?
turns.zh: 如果你出于你刚阐述的这些原因，拥有一套横跨所有这些不同武器系统的一体化架构，那么究竟是谁做出——或者说拥有——那个击杀决定（kill decision）？是谁决定针对哪些目标、所有这些不同手段的部署实际上是什么样子？而且我猜大多数时候你都是在高度受压的时间环境下运作的，对吧？

turns.en: Yes, absolutely.
turns.zh: 是的，当然。

turns.en: Normally, it's known as the Target Execution Authority, the TEA. The military does a phenomenal job at identifying this well before a conflict when you go forward. Depending on what type of threat that is, it's going to say you have the authorities at your level to accomplish the following things. If you are an infantry battalion commander, you're a lieutenant colonel, and you have your soldiers out there on the battlefield, you're only going to have a certain amount of authorities. Your rules of engagement are going to stop at a specific level. But then as it goes further and further up, what they call the operational command, the operational command, so if you're looking at the Iran scenario, a lot of those have been delegated down to U.S.
turns.zh: 通常它被称为目标执行权（Target Execution Authority，TEA）。军队在冲突开始之前、在你向前推进之前，就会把这件事识别得非常清楚。取决于那是哪种类型的威胁，它会说明你在你的层级上拥有完成以下事项的权限。如果你是一名步兵营营长（infantry battalion commander），你是名 lieutenant colonel（中校），你的士兵在战场上，你只会拥有有限的一些权限，你的交战规则（rules of engagement）会止步于某个特定层级。但再往上，也就是他们所说的作战指挥（operational command），所以如果你看 Iran 那个场景，很多权限已经被下放给了 U.S.

turns.en: CENTCOM. U.S. CENTCOM, U.S.
turns.zh: CENTCOM。U.S. CENTCOM，U.S.

turns.en: Central Command, delegates quite a bit to Fifth Fleet so that the U.S. Navy can answer those questions. So if you have a laser onboard a U.S. Navy vessel as part of the George Washington or the Abraham Lincoln carrier strike group, then they will know at their level what they're allowed to do and what they're not.
turns.zh: 中央司令部（Central Command）把相当多的权限下放给了第五舰队（Fifth Fleet），好让 U.S. Navy 能回答那些问题。所以如果你在 U.S. Navy 的一艘舰艇上有一门激光，作为 George Washington 或 Abraham Lincoln 航母打击群（carrier strike group）的一部分，那么他们在自己这个层级上就会知道自己被允许做什么、不被允许做什么。

turns.en: And that's going to be determined based off of that. So it changes.
turns.zh: 而这就会基于那一点来决定。所以它会变化。

turns.en: I don't want to say that it's always going to be the following, but the military knows at that point in time. They also know that they have the right to self-defense. So that is always priority number one, no matter how you're looking at it. But normally there will be a There will be a ship captain. There will be a carrier strike group, you know, admiral that will will have that specific authority.
turns.zh: 我不想说它永远都会是以下这样，但军队在那个时刻是知道的。他们也知道自己有自卫权（right to self-defense），所以那永远是第一优先，无论你怎么看。但通常会有——会有一名舰长，会有一名航母打击群的、你知道，海军上将（admiral），拥有那个特定权限。

turns.en: And so when he sees it. Right.
turns.zh: 所以当他看到它的时候。对吧。

turns.en: So part of what they end up doing is they put all this stuff into the Aegis system and they can see all of those. There will be a common operational picture. And based off of that, that admiral can make that decision.
turns.zh: 所以他们最终做的一部分，是把这些东西全都放进 Aegis 系统里，他们能看到所有这些。会有一个通用作战图（common operational picture），基于此，那位海军上将就能做出那个决定。

turns.en: What makes a weapon system exquisite? I hear this term from time to time in these conferences, and I realize I actually don't know the answer to that.
turns.zh: 是什么让一套武器系统称得上'精密'（exquisite）？我在这些会议上时不时听到这个词，而我意识到自己其实并不知道答案。

turns.en: So normally, it really just comes down to the sophistication and technology that is included in it. So if you're looking at an interceptor, if it is an exquisite interceptor, it means you have the top-of-the-line seeker technology that is inside the payload, inside the front of that interceptor, because... You're trying to shoot a bullet down with a bullet at that point in time, right? The science that's behind that is phenomenal because you have to be able to see exactly where that threat is coming from and whether or not now you're getting into maneuverable systems as well, right? It's not just always a 100% path. I'm flying directly at you, never going to switch path. so these seekers have to be able to then not only do it, they have to identify and track, but then they also have to then do adjust to whatever changes in those paths also come. So that is an exquisite interceptor type of, of munition. If you have long range precision munitions that we are firing offensively, same thing kind of applies. It has to do with how fast it goes, whether or not the tail fins maneuver these and cause it to, uh, to change course as well, because now we're trying to also then avoid enemy air defense systems as well, so that we can make sure that we hit the target as well. So the payload that's on it, how fast, how big of an explosion are you trying to achieve? All of those things play into that exquisite munitions perspective.
turns.zh: 通常，它真的就归结为其中包含的精密程度和技术。所以如果你看一枚拦截弹，如果它是一枚精密拦截弹，那就意味着你在弹头内、在那枚拦截弹的前端，拥有最顶尖的导引头（seeker）技术，因为在那个时刻你是在试图用一颗子弹去击落另一颗子弹，对吧？这背后的科学非常了不起，因为你必须能够精确看到那个威胁从哪儿来，而且现在你是否还进入了可机动（maneuverable）系统的问题，对吧？它并不总是 100% 一条直线径直朝你飞来、永不改变路径。所以这些导引头不仅要能做到这一点，要能识别和追踪，还必须对那些路径中出现的任何变化做出调整。所以那就是一种精密拦截弹类型的弹药。如果你有我们进攻性发射的远程精确弹药（long range precision munitions），同样的道理也大致适用。这关系到它飞得多快，尾翼（tail fins）是否会机动、让它改变航向，因为现在我们也试图避开敌方的防空系统，好确保我们能命中目标。所以它上面的弹头、它有多快、你想实现多大的爆炸——所有这些都构成了那个精密弹药的视角。

turns.en: Got it.
turns.zh: 明白了。

turns.en: The other side is the gravity bombs. Gravity bombs are just standard GPS guided munitions, where as long as you can get over the target and you drop that, It's very, very simple maneuvering and all that. It's a lot less because you're not worried so much about the energetics behind it, and you're really just letting it hit the targets.
turns.zh: 另一侧是重力炸弹（gravity bombs）。重力炸弹就是标准的 GPS 制导弹药，只要你能飞到目标上方把它投下去，它的机动等等都非常非常简单。它要便宜得多，因为你不用那么担心它背后的能量学（energetics），你真的只是让它去命中目标。

turns.en: Aren't all bombs gravity in the end? I mean, they all have to fall back to Earth eventually. Okay, anyway, to what extent do military commanders take into account economic costs when they're making these operational decisions? Would someone hesitate to press the button on launching a bunch of ballistic missiles because they're thinking about how much it might cost the U.S.
turns.zh: 说到底，难道所有炸弹不都是靠重力的吗？我是说，它们最终都得落回地球。好，不管怎样，军事指挥官在做这些作战决定时，会在多大程度上考虑经济成本？会不会有人因为想着这可能要让 U.S.

turns.en: Government.
turns.zh: 政府（Government）。

turns.en: And I'm thinking back to, I'm sure we've all seen Top Gun when Maverick crashes the airplane or whatever, and his commander is like chewing him out and saying, that's not your plane. It's not your money. It's the taxpayer's plane and the taxpayer's money. Does that factor into actual operational decisions at all?
turns.zh: 我就想起——我相信我们都看过 Top Gun——Maverick 把飞机坠毁了还是怎么的，他的指挥官就骂他，说，那不是你的飞机，那不是你的钱，那是纳税人的飞机、纳税人的钱。这种考量会哪怕一点点地进入实际的作战决定吗？

turns.en: So I think the best way, you described it perfectly. And I think that that actually shows how great the military system is, is because if you are a tactical commander, And you have if you're in that situation, all that you are going to use whatever is necessary to protect your force.
turns.zh: 我觉得最好的方式——你描述得非常到位。我认为那其实恰恰体现了军队体系有多出色，因为如果你是一名战术指挥官（tactical commander），处在那种情境下，你所要做的就是动用一切必要手段去保护你的部队。

turns.en: Doesn't matter.
turns.zh: 无所谓。

turns.en: You have the operational command and you have those abilities as you get farther up the food chain, as you become those flag officers. those general officers, right, the admirals and the generals, when you start getting to those operational higher level of command decisions— they're the ones who are tied more into the national. So you have tactical, operational, strategic, and national authorities. And so as you get closer into those strategic and national authorities, that's when those leaders are the ones who start looking at that and saying, I need systems where I'm not spending $ 4. 1 million to shoot down a $ 30, 000 drone. But that is not something that your standard. Lieutenant or captain or major is dealing with at their level.
turns.zh: 你有作战指挥，而当你往食物链更上层走、成为那些将官（flag officers）、那些将军（general officers），对吧，那些海军上将和将军时，你就拥有那些能力；当你开始触及那些更高层级的作战指挥决定时——他们才是与国家层面联系更紧的人。所以你有战术（tactical）、作战（operational）、战略（strategic）和国家（national）这几级权限。当你越接近战略和国家层面权限时，就是那些领导者开始去看这个、并说'我需要一套系统，让我不用花 410 万美元去击落一架 3 万美元的无人机'的时候。但那不是一个普通的 lieutenant（中尉）、captain（上尉）或 major（少校）在他们那个层级上要处理的事。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: I would imagine, though, that they're not thinking about, oh, what is this going to cost the taxpayer? But they are still fundamentally having to think about economizing. They have a certain amount of capacity with them at any given moment. And they have to think, when are they going to use their more scarce weapons that probably does cost more, but scarce weapons. So we have this problem. Everyone's talked about it. the war in Iran, this rapid depletion of very expensive stocks, where would we have to get to with some of the weapon systems you're talking about such that, or where are we on the path such that these technologies could meaningfully change some of the economics so that we could accomplish some of the same goals that we want while on the very abstract level saving money but just generally speaking, solve this problem of ours of munitions depletement?
turns.zh: 不过我会想，他们并不是在想'哦，这要花纳税人多少钱'，但他们从根本上仍然必须考虑节约（economizing）。他们在任何给定时刻随身携带的容量（capacity）是有限的，他们必须想清楚，什么时候才动用他们那些更稀缺的武器——那些武器大概也更贵，但重点是稀缺。所以我们碰到了这个问题，人人都在谈——就是 Iran 那场战争，非常昂贵的库存被迅速耗尽。对于你说的这些武器系统，我们得走到哪一步——或者说我们现在处在这条路的什么位置——这些技术才能有意义地改变其中一些经济性，让我们既能实现我们想要的一些目标，又能在非常抽象的层面上省钱，但更泛泛地说，是解决我们这个弹药耗尽的问题？

turns.en: Yeah, no, I think we're in the middle of it right now, because when you look at how the military is structured and how the Department of War, Department of Defense is right now pushing some of these additional, what they call the multi-year framework agreements for these munitions platforms, they're doing that because they're trying to, they're recognizing right now that it has been, I don't want to call it a failure of economies of force, but you know, the U.S. military has focused so long on looking at the peer type fight. So this has been a lesson learned for the military to say, hey, look, I right now, as you even mentioned, here is my arsenal. This is what I have available to.
turns.zh: 是的，我觉得我们现在正处在这个过程之中，因为当你看军队是如何组织的，看战争部（Department of War）/国防部（Department of Defense）现在是如何推动这些额外的、他们称之为多年期框架协议（multi-year framework agreements）的弹药平台时，他们这么做，是因为他们现在正认识到，这一直是——我不想称之为'兵力经济（economies of force）的失败'，但你知道，U.S. 军队长久以来一直专注于盯着同级对手（peer）那种战斗。所以对军队来说这是一次经验教训，让他们说，嘿，看，就像你甚至提到的，现在这是——这是我的军火库，这是我此刻

turns.en: Me right now.
turns.zh: 我此刻手头可用的东西。

turns.en: And I'm getting shot at right now. I'm getting I'm getting attacked by Fatah 110 ballistic missiles. I'm getting shot. I'm getting attacked by Shaheed 136 drones. And hey, the what I have at my at my fingertips right now, our PAC-3 interceptors from the Patriot system.
turns.zh: 而我此刻正被射击，我正遭到 Fatah 110 弹道导弹的攻击，我正被射击，我正遭到 Shahed 136 无人机的攻击。而嘿，我此刻手边就有的，是来自 Patriot 系统的 PAC-3 拦截弹。

turns.en: That's what I have.
turns.zh: 这就是我有的。

turns.en: And so therefore, that's what I'm going to use. The Navy's looking at it and they're like, well, I've got SM-3s, I've got SM-6s. And so that's what I am using. And so what you're seeing right now is, hey, we don't want to do that. That's been the demand signal to industry right now is that low cost containerized munitions, those low cost interceptors, the high-powered microwave, high-energy laser, the urgency and demand for some of these systems is because exactly what you're saying is I want at my level, if I was sitting right now and I was still Colonel Sanders, KFC, sitting in and I'm working with my force, I want to have all of the solutions so that I have more options at my fingertips. I want to have more arrows in my quiver so that I can make the decision between electronic warfare, high-powered microwave, high-energy laser, guns cheap interceptors as well as exquisite missiles i want to have all of those things at my fingertips and that's what we're at right now.
turns.zh: 所以我就要用它。Navy 看着它，心想，嗯，我有 SM-3，我有 SM-6，所以那就是我在用的。因此你现在看到的是：嘿，我们不想那样做。这就是此刻传递给工业界的需求信号（demand signal）——低成本、容器化（containerized）的弹药，那些低成本拦截弹，高功率微波、高能激光，对这些系统的紧迫性和需求，正是因为你说的那点：如果我是坐在这儿、还是 Colonel Sanders（KFC 那位）、和我的部队一起共事，我想在我这个层级上拥有所有的解决方案，好让我手边有更多选项。我想箭袋里有更多箭，这样我就能在电子战（electronic warfare）、高功率微波、高能激光、gun、廉价拦截弹以及精密导弹之间做决定。我想把所有这些东西都握在手边，而这正是我们此刻所处的状态。

turns.en: How easy or difficult is it to actually produce these things at scale? Because a couple of familiar names kept coming up when I was researching this. Rare earths, including gallium. And this one is unfamiliar to me. Joe, do you know what ytterbium is?
turns.zh: 要真正大规模（at scale）生产这些东西有多容易或多难？因为我在研究这个的时候，有几个熟悉的名字不断冒出来。稀土（rare earths），包括镓（gallium）。还有一个我不熟悉的。Joe，你知道 ytterbium（镱）是什么吗？

turns.en: Ytterbium?
turns.zh: Ytterbium？

turns.en: Ytterbium? Why ytterbium? I think it's ytterbium.
turns.zh: Ytterbium？为什么是 ytterbium？我觉得它念 ytterbium。

turns.en: No.
turns.zh: 不对。

turns.en: Keep going.
turns.zh: 继续说。

turns.en: All right.
turns.zh: 好吧。

turns.en: Well, both of them. as is tradition, are mostly produced by China. So it seems like if you want to ramp up production of these things, even if you agree that these are effective weapons and they're going to do a lot for defensive capabilities, scaling up production could still be a challenge.
turns.zh: 嗯，这两样，按照惯例，都主要由中国生产。所以看起来，如果你想扩大这些东西的产量，即便你同意它们是有效的武器、会为防御能力带来很大提升，扩大生产规模仍然可能是个挑战。

turns.en: No, it absolutely is.
turns.zh: 不，这绝对是个挑战。

turns.en: When you look at critical minerals across, there's terbium, like you mentioned. There's dysprosium. Dysprosium is another one that a lot of people use. Military uses a lot of neodymium boron iron magnets. And the fact that I know that off the top of my head just shows how many times we've had to go over this.
turns.zh: 当你通盘看关键矿产（critical minerals）时，有铽（terbium），就像你提到的；有镝（dysprosium），镝是另一个很多人用的；军队大量使用钕硼铁磁体（neodymium boron iron magnets）。而我能张口就来这些，恰恰说明我们得反复过这块内容多少遍了。

turns.en: But, yeah, so critical minerals becomes very, very key.
turns.zh: 但是，Yeah，所以关键矿产就变得非常非常关键。

turns.en: And so when you start looking at some of the deals that are being made by the Department of War– right now is a great example of that, right? The deal with MP materials to actually, you know, gain a piece of ground specifically inside the U.S.
turns.zh: 所以当你开始看战争部（Department of War）现在正在敲定的一些交易时，那就是一个绝佳的例子，对吧？比如和 MP Materials 的那笔交易，去真正地——你知道——在美国国内拿到一块地，

turns.en: For domestic onshoring of these capabilities. But you're absolutely right.
turns.zh: 用于把这些能力回流（onshoring）到国内。但你说得完全没错。

turns.en: There are quite a few of these critical minerals that China has a predominance in the world. They have, you know, sometimes 85, even 90 percent of the supply chain. So how important it is that we're using the ones that we have correctly and When China last year added 12 critical minerals that they were not going to share with the United States. You know, these are some of the key ones, like you said. And so the nice thing is that a lot of the defense primes have recognized this as a risk for quite a while. And so they've already been working towards some of these. But the bigger problem now is these are not just critical minerals that are used for defense platforms. These are a lot of dual-use capabilities with a lot of civilian and commercial needs as well. And so if you're looking at a brushless motor for a drone, that could be used for a civilian drone, or it could be used for a military Reaper drone or a Global Hawk. And so when you start looking at those, it is a lot of decisions that have to be made by industry.
turns.zh: 有相当多的这些关键矿产，中国在全世界占据主导地位，它们有时掌握着供应链的 85%、甚至 90%。所以我们能否正确地用好我们手头拥有的那些，就非常重要。而当中国去年新增了 12 种他们不打算与美国分享的关键矿产时——你知道，这些正是其中的一些关键的，就像你说的。所以好的一点是，很多国防主承包商（defense primes）早就把这当成一种风险来认识了，所以他们一直已经在朝这些方向努力。但现在更大的问题是，这些不只是用于国防平台的关键矿产，它们很多是两用（dual-use）能力，还有大量的民用和商业需求。所以如果你看一个无人机的无刷电机（brushless motor），它既可以用在民用无人机上，也可以用在军用的 Reaper 无人机或 Global Hawk 上。所以当你开始看这些时，工业界需要做很多决定。

turns.en: By the way, I have to let listeners know who've been listening for a while. I found my tungsten cube thanks to Tracy. I had been missing it, and she suggested a drawer that we store stuff in that it might be in, and it was there, so thank you. Turns out you can buy a terbium cube.
turns.zh: 顺便说一句，我得让听了一阵子的听众知道，多亏了 Tracy，我找到了我的钨立方（tungsten cube）。我之前一直找不着，她建议我去我们存放东西的某个抽屉里找找看，它就在那儿，所以谢谢她。结果发现你还能买到一个铽立方（terbium cube）。

turns.en: Oh, no. No, no, no.
turns.zh: 哦，不。不不不。

turns.en: It's $ 40 for a little 10-millimeter cube. I don't know. Does it look nice?
turns.zh: 一个 10 毫米的小立方要 40 美元。我不知道。它好看吗？

turns.en: It's just silvery.
turns.zh: 它就是银色的。

turns.en: Yeah, it's just a silvery cube. I'm curious, like, when, like... Maybe a big picture, when a sort of new type of weapons regime, sort of maybe disruptive weapons tech emerges, in your seat as an analyst, how much of this is coming from the Primes, and how much of this is coming from... Defense startups, etc. There's like some defense startup is like, you know, we don't have an exquisite missile system that we want to keep selling. And therefore, we're not going to fall captive to the innovators dilemma, unlike a defense prime that may not be as motivated to push on a technology that could, you know, render their existing workhorse sales to be. less market competitive. What are you seeing in terms of market dynamics here?
turns.zh: Yeah，它就是个银色的立方体。我很好奇，就是，什么时候……也许从大局看，当一种新型武器体系、某种也许是颠覆性的武器技术出现时，站在你这个分析师的位置上，这其中有多少来自主承包商（Primes），又有多少来自……国防初创公司（defense startups）之类的。就是说，某个国防初创公司会想，你知道，我们并没有一个想继续卖出去的精密导弹系统，因此我们不会沦为创新者窘境（innovator's dilemma）的俘虏，而不像某个国防主承包商，可能没那么有动力去推进一项技术——那项技术可能让他们现有的主力产品销量变得市场竞争力更弱。在市场动态这块，你看到了什么？

turns.en: No, it is a great point because you're hitting on something that the DOW has actually identified now and has started to push towards as well. The defense primes right now are scaling. We've already talked about the exquisite munitions, right? And so a lot of the multi-year framework agreements that have come to them has been to increase the stockpiles of things that we already have. So PAC-3 interceptors going from 620 a year to 2000 per year. That is what they're pushing for. That's a 3.3x increase on what they're doing. The THAAD system, the Terminal High Altitude Air Defense System, these are like $ 12 to $ 15 million per interceptor.
turns.zh: 不，这是个很好的点，因为你戳中了战争部（DOW）现在其实已经识别出来、并开始朝之推进的东西。国防主承包商此刻正在扩产（scaling）。我们已经谈过精密弹药了，对吧？所以很多来到他们面前的多年期框架协议，都是为了增加我们已经有的那些东西的库存。所以 PAC-3 拦截弹从每年 620 枚增加到每年 2000 枚，那正是他们在推动的，那是他们在做的事情上的 3.3 倍增长。THAAD 系统，也就是末段高空区域防御系统（Terminal High Altitude Air Defense System），这些拦截弹每枚大约 1200 万到 1500 万美元。

turns.en: They're trying to increase that 4x.
turns.zh: 他们正试图把它提高 4 倍。

turns.en: And then you've got the Precision Strike Munition, which is a long-range offensive system that we've used in Iran successfully that's very strategic to a China fight. That is one that they're trying to increase by up to 4x as well. So you start putting those together. That's your exquisite munitions piece. But that middle ground that I was talking about, right, where you're looking for these low-cost containerized munitions, you're looking for, okay, I don't have, I'm not ready to just do a high-powered microwave, but I don't want to use a $ 4 million interceptor. There are contracts that are out right now, specifically five companies, Coaspire, Leidos, Anduril, Zone 5, and Castilian are the five contracting companies right now that the DoD has contracted with and say, I need this middle ground solution.
turns.zh: 然后你还有精确打击弹药（Precision Strike Munition），那是一种远程进攻性系统，我们在 Iran 成功用过，对一场对华（China）战斗非常有战略意义。那也是他们正试图提高多达 4 倍的一个。所以你把那些拼在一起，那就是你的精密弹药那块。但我之前说的那个中间地带，对吧——你在找这些低成本、容器化的弹药，你在找'好，我还没准备好直接上高功率微波，但我不想用一发 400 万美元的拦截弹'。现在有一些合同已经出来了，具体是五家公司：Coaspire、Leidos、Anduril、Zone 5 和 Castilian，是国防部（DoD）现在签约的五家承包公司，说'我需要这个中间地带的解决方案，

turns.en: I need tens of thousands of these.
turns.zh: 我需要数以万计的这种。

turns.en: Not trying to jump, like I said, from 620 to 2,000 or 96 to 400 for the THAAD system. We're talking about, I need thousands, tens of thousands. That's my demand signal. Let's make this happen. And so the market, these disruptors are the ones who are picking up those contracts. So the short term, the primes are winning because they already have the production lines They are able to put these contracts directly into place, and they're pushing for it. But that mid-grade, think about three to five years, the scalability for the Andurals and the Castilians of the world to come in and grab that middle market as well is an area that the primes aren't looking to grab into too much. and they're allowing some of these tech disruptors to do it, but you're also seeing a lot of joint ventures as well across the board, not only internally to the US, but also our partnerships around the world. Lockheed does a great job, so does RTX, partnering with some European companies as well, Rheinmetall being one of them, so that they can start to increase capacity overseas as well.
turns.zh: 不是像我说的，试图从 620 跳到 2000，或者 THAAD 系统从 96 跳到 400。我们说的是，我需要成千上万、数以万计。那就是我的需求信号。让我们把它做成。所以市场——这些颠覆者（disruptors）正是接过这些合同的人。所以短期内，主承包商在赢，因为他们已经有生产线，他们能够把这些合同直接落地，而且他们在推动这件事。但那个中端——想想三到五年——像 Anduril、Castilian 这类公司的可扩展性（scalability），去进来抓住那个中间市场，也是主承包商不太想去过多涉足的一个领域，他们就允许其中一些技术颠覆者去做。但你同时也看到很多合资企业（joint ventures）遍地开花，不仅在美国内部，还有我们在世界各地的伙伴关系。Lockheed 做得很好，RTX 也是，跟一些欧洲公司合作，Rheinmetall 就是其中之一，好让他们也能开始在海外扩大产能。

turns.en: Can you talk a little bit more about AI and safety issues when it comes to this kind of weaponry? Because Joe and I, we've been having a lot of conversations recently about LLMs and some recent safety incidents, including an open AI model escaping its sandbox during a test and hacking into Hugging Face, which is like bad enough. But then when you think about AI potentially in a military environment and maybe having access to a bunch of ballistic missiles or now laser beams, that seems kind of terrifying.
turns.zh: 你能再多谈谈这类武器涉及的 AI 和安全（safety）问题吗？因为 Joe 和我最近一直在大量讨论 LLM 以及一些近期的安全事件，包括一个 OpenAI 的模型在一次测试中逃出了它的沙盒（sandbox）、黑进了 Hugging Face——这本身就够糟糕了。但你再想想 AI 有可能处在军事环境里，也许能接触到一大堆弹道导弹、或者现在是激光束，那似乎有点可怕。

turns.en: No, absolutely.
turns.zh: 不，确实如此。

turns.en: And funny enough, when I was at war college, my group did an entire thing about AI and levels of trust because you really are looking at a lot of the stuff that you're originally seeing partnered into the Pentagon right now is things that are going to help us do our staff jobs better. Let's look at how to be able to optimize processes. How do we do a better job of tagging our capabilities so that we can track them better and so on and so forth? What it hasn't entered into very much is really when you look at identifying friend and foe leading to a command decision for a tactical strike. Those are things that are still maintained. Those are human in the loop AI problems. And so that's really where you're seeing a lot from the military side right now is I want you to help me clean up the noise. You see a lot of that on the imagery intelligence side of the house and saying, okay, I want AI to be able to look through a lot of my platforms.
turns.zh: 有意思的是，我在战争学院（war college）时，我们小组做过一整个关于 AI 和信任层级（levels of trust）的课题。因为你真正在看的、你最初看到被引入 Pentagon 的很多东西，都是那些能帮我们把参谋工作（staff jobs）做得更好的东西。我们来看看如何优化流程，我们如何更好地给能力打标签（tagging）以便更好地追踪它们，等等诸如此类。它还没怎么进入的领域，真的是当你看识别敌我（friend and foe）、进而引向一个战术打击的指挥决定时。那些仍然是由人来掌控的，那些是'人在回路'（human in the loop）的 AI 问题。所以那真的是你现在从军队这边看到很多的地方：我想让你帮我清理噪音。你在图像情报（imagery intelligence）那一侧看到很多这种，说'好，我想让 AI 能筛查我的很多平台，

turns.en: I want to take all the satellite imagery.
turns.zh: 我想把所有的卫星图像（satellite imagery），

turns.en: I want you to help me normalize this and help me see where the change detections may be. Pickaxe Mountain would be a good example of that, right? I'm using it as a theoretical, but let's say we wanted to focus on everything and anything that's going around Pickaxe Mountain for the nuclear Iran discussion. So AI could potentially do that from an imagery perspective to say, all right, I've watched the videos for 12 to 16 hours, and based off of it, this is what we have. And you can flag an alert, but that alert for something that's going to happen, maybe it's a dump truck driving away, and that's what you told it to look for. great, but there's still going to be a human that's looking at that then. When that alert comes on, there's an analyst that's sitting there. There's a commander that would make a decision behind that that says, this is what I want to do about that truck that is driving away. Where we are not at right now and where we are quite a ways away based off of trust models and all that, I think exactly where we should be is we are not at the point where AI is going to go, I see that truck, I've been given an order to destroy it, and I am going to take that target execution authority that I mentioned earlier, and just drop the bomb.
turns.zh: 我想让你帮我把它标准化（normalize），帮我看出变化检测（change detections）可能在哪里。Pickaxe Mountain 会是个好例子，对吧？我把它当作一个理论假设，但假设我们想聚焦于 Pickaxe Mountain 周围的一切、任何东西，用于 Iran 核问题的讨论。所以 AI 有可能从图像的角度去做那件事，说'好，我已经看了 12 到 16 小时的视频，据此，这是我们掌握的情况'。你可以标记一个警报，但那个关于某件将要发生之事的警报，也许它只是一辆自卸卡车（dump truck）开走了，而那正是你让它去留意的东西。很好，但那时仍然会有一个人来看这个。当那个警报响起时，坐在那儿的是一名分析师，会有一名指挥官在其后做出决定，说'关于那辆开走的卡车，这是我想做的'。我们现在还没到、而且基于信任模型等等我们还差得比较远的地步——我认为恰恰是我们应该处的位置——是：我们还没到 AI 会说'我看到那辆卡车了，我接到了摧毁它的命令，我要接过我之前提到的那个目标执行权，然后直接投弹'的地步。

turns.en: So Wayne, I'm looking at one of your most recent research notes on the Bloomberg terminal, and you talk about the directed energy market growing two to three times from where it's at currently, which is $ 6 to $ 8 billion, and that's over the next decade. And I just want to be clear, is that a forecast for like actual procurement, or is that including R & D on the whole? Because it seems like so far, most of the money that's been spent has been on development.
turns.zh: Wayne，我在 Bloomberg 终端（Bloomberg terminal）上看你最近的一份研究笔记，你谈到定向能市场会从目前的 60 亿到 80 亿美元增长两到三倍，而且那是在未来十年内。我想先弄清楚，那是一个针对实际采购（procurement）的预测，还是把研发（R&D）整个都算进去了？因为看起来到目前为止，花掉的大部分钱都在开发上。

turns.en: Absolutely.
turns.zh: 确实。

turns.en: I mean, we have spent over $ 15 billion on the R & D up until this point, specifically to get to where we're at right now. And it is a good news story because it is transitioning to procurement. You are starting to see that as different portions. The Army, like I mentioned earlier, about the striker vehicles, the 50 kilowatt laser platforms and all that. You're starting to see that start showing up inside of the multi-domain task forces. You're seeing the Navy continue to push for additional high-energy laser solutions. Contracts with Epirus, one of the companies that does some high-powered microwave stuff, is tied directly into both the Army and to the Marine Corps because of their capabilities to protect against drone swarms. And they've even developed something called the Leonidas H2O system, which helps you know, disabled boat motors. So when you start looking at some of the tactical problems that you run into in the Black Sea and the Red Sea and all that for just even remote controlled fast boats, you know, trying to go after blue water Navy assets that cost, you know, hundreds of millions, if not billions of dollars, having these types of capabilities are exactly what you're looking for. So right now is some of the transition from the R & D side into the procurement market.
turns.zh: 我是说，到目前为止我们在研发上已经花了超过 150 亿美元，专门就是为了走到我们现在所处的位置。而这是个好消息，因为它正在转向采购（procurement）。你开始看到那作为不同的部分显现出来。Army，就像我前面提到的 striker 车辆、50 千瓦激光平台等等，你开始看到它出现在多域特遣队（multi-domain task forces）里。你看到 Navy 持续推动更多的高能激光方案。与 Epirus 的合同——那是做高功率微波的公司之一——直接同时和 Army 以及 Marine Corps 挂钩，因为他们有能力防御无人机蜂群。他们甚至开发了一个叫 Leonidas H2O 的系统，能帮助——你知道——让船的马达失灵。所以当你开始看你在 Black Sea 和 Red Sea 等地碰到的一些战术问题时，哪怕只是遥控快艇（fast boats）试图去攻击那些造价数亿、甚至数十亿美元的蓝水海军（blue water Navy）资产，拥有这类能力正是你想要的。所以现在是研发那一侧向采购市场过渡的时期。

turns.en: But you are correct.
turns.zh: 但你说得对。

turns.en: There still is a lot more R & D because if you look at the research and engineering department from the Pentagon, they're looking for a one megawatt laser by 2030. The science continues to go, right? It's really a question as to whether or not the physics and the science behind can continue to support and bring down those size, weight, and power requirements necessary to be able to produce.
turns.zh: 研发还有很多，因为如果你看 Pentagon 的研究与工程部门，他们要在 2030 年前搞出一台一兆瓦（one megawatt）的激光。科学仍在推进，对吧？这真的是一个问题：其背后的物理学和科学能否继续支撑下去，并把那些必要的尺寸、重量和功率要求降下来，以便能够生产。

turns.en: It i have to say and i've said this on many episodes i do not have great intuitions for any time we're talking about units of electricity whether it's megawatt or megawatt hours the context of a grid can you give me an when you say they're looking for a one megawatt laser What is that? How should I conceptualize this? What's a metaphor that I could use to understand what that would mean?
turns.zh: 我不得不说——我在很多期节目里都说过——每当我们谈论电力单位时，无论是兆瓦（megawatt）还是兆瓦时（megawatt hours），在电网（grid）的语境下，我都没有很好的直觉。你能不能给我一个——当你说他们想要一台一兆瓦的激光时，那是什么？我该怎么去概念化它？有什么比喻能让我理解那意味着什么？

turns.en: Yeah.
turns.zh: Yeah。

turns.en: So right now, the 50 kilowatt laser is capable of if a drone is flying at you, you should be able to knock that drone down at one time.
turns.zh: 现在，那台 50 千瓦的激光，如果一架无人机朝你飞来，你应该能够一次就把那架无人机打下来。

turns.en: Right.
turns.zh: 对。

turns.en: From a kilowatt perspective, when you start looking at one megawatt, you're trying to create a beam that is so strong that you can shoot down something that is flying at you at. you know, 1,000 miles an hour, potentially up to 4,000 to 5,000 miles an hour, as is a Mach 5 hypersonic weapon would.
turns.zh: 从千瓦的角度看，当你开始研究一兆瓦时，你是在试图制造一束强到可以击落一个正以——你知道——每小时 1,000 英里、乃至高达每小时 4,000 到 5,000 英里飞来的东西的光束，就像一件 Mach 5 的高超音速武器那样。

turns.en: And the gap between getting from 50 kilowatt to one megawatt, is that on the sort of energy side that's on the side of the laser? Is it a technology that exploits that much energy? Like, what needs to be solved to make that jump?
turns.zh: 而从 50 千瓦到一兆瓦之间的这段差距，是在能量那一侧、在激光那一侧吗？是一种能利用那么多能量的技术吗？就是说，要实现那一跃，需要解决什么？

turns.en: Yeah, I would say it's almost an iterative thing right now. DARPA is looking for higher level of solutions. They're looking for almost a revolution in military affairs because they want to jump iterations or increments in terms of what that development is. But I think it's a little bit of all of those, right? Part of it is on the physics side of the house to be able to generate one megawatt and keep the beam where you want it to be. But then also, it's also deployability discussion. Having a one megawatt laser that is static because you need to plug it into shore power is limited in a certain aspect. It is great for self-defense and force protection. So think about it in terms of putting it on a military base in Kuwait. That would be a great opportunity to be able to do it because that is a shore power solution with a fairly unlimited magazine that's attached to it. But when you start looking at a potential peer adversary threat where you want to be able to move your forces forward and you have to contend with these types of missiles being shot at you, it's very difficult to carry around a generator that can produce a one megawatt capability that you then use to create these impulse beams.
